Adolescents prone to risk-taking frequently underestimate injury probability, attributing adverse outcomes to “bad luck” rather than behavioral choices30, creating a dangerous perceptual gap between action and consequence. Critically, the estimation of athletic ability—the subjective evaluation of one’s physical and technical capabilities—serves as a pivotal psychological mediator influencing both risk perception and behavioral choices9,27. Prior research presents contradictory findings: some studies associate ability overestimation with increased injury risk through reckless behaviors8,9, while others paradoxically link underestimation to elevated risk via compromised self-confidence and movement hesitation 27. These inconsistencies likely stem from methodological limitations in prior work, which predominantly employed cross-sectional designs and failed to differentiate between self-ratings and external evaluations. Most notably, Kontos’ seminal 2004 study examined ability estimation primarily in children under 14 years using retrospective injury reporting—limiting causal inference and developmental applicability to adolescent populations27. This study addresses three critical gaps in literature. First, no prospective investigation has examined the Athletic Ability Discrepancy Score—quantified as the divergence between self- and coach ratings of athletic ability—as an independent predictor of match-related injuries in adolescent soccer players. Second, existing research has failed to simultaneously model the interplay among recovery quality, risk-taking behaviors, and other self- rating discrepancies within an integrated predictive framework. Third, the majority of prior studies focused exclusively on physiological determinants or employed cross-sectional designs ill-suited for establishing temporal precedence between risk factors and injury outcomes. Accordingly, this prospective cohort study investigates the combined influence of psychological (mental fatigue, perceived injury risk, risk-taking behaviors, Ath

Baseline measurements To establish baseline data, a comprehensive questionnaire was administered to adolescent soccer players, structured into three key sections: demographic information, soccer training profile, and history of previous injuries. The researcher conducted individual interviews to complete the questionnaire, which included questions about participants’ age, height, weight, soccer experience, duration of training sessions, and session frequency. Additionally, a self-reported injury history questionnaire was completed collaboratively by both the adolescent players and their parents/guardians to document participants’ previous soccer-related injuries and their locations. This information was also used to confirm that all players were injury-free at the time of study enrollment. A second structured questionnaire, administered via a separate online link, was used to assess various psychological and behavioral variables including mental fatigue, Total Quality Recovery (TQR), Perceived Match Load (session-RPE), perceived sports ability, injury risk perception, and risk-taking behaviors. Perceived match load was calculated after each match by multiplying the session duration (in minutes) by the perceived match intensity, measured using the Borg 6–20 Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale, where higher values indicate greater workload32. Recovery quality was evaluated using the TQR scale, comprising two components: TQR Perceived, a subjective rating ranging from 6 (very poor recovery) to 20 (very good recovery), modeled after the Borg RPE scale; and TQR Action, an objective score based on factors such as nutrition, sleep, rest, and emotional support, with a maximum total score of 2016. Mental fatigue was assessed using a Visual Analog Scale (V AS), on which participants rated their fatigue level from 0 (“Not at all”) to 10 (“Completely fatigued”), following the protocol described by Habay, et al. 33. Perceived injury risk was measured through an adapted three-item scale, where players rated their perceived chance of injury during a match (1 = no chance, 5 = certain), susceptibility to injury (1 = not susceptible, 5 = very susceptible), and estimated likelihood of injury occurrence (1 = < 10%, 5 = 100%)24,34. Risk-taking behaviors were assessed using a three-item scale, evaluating agreement with statements regarding irresponsible behavior, cautiousness (reverse-scored), and peers’ attitudes towards risk-taking during matches. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with final scores averaged35. Athletic ability was evaluated through both player self-ratings and coach ratings using a five-point Likert scale (1 = very low to 5 = very high) relative to same-age peers. The Athletic Ability Discrepancy Score was computed as Self-rating minus Coach rating of athletic ability. A positive score indicates the player rated themselves higher than the coach (potential overestimation), while a negative score indicates the player rated themselves lower (potential underestimation)27. Notably, a positive mean discrepancy score across the sample reflects a systematic tendency among adolescent athletes to rate their athletic abilities more favorably than their coach, rather than indicating universal overestimation of objective ability. To ensure data integrity and minimize peer influence, data collection was conducted individually in a private, controlled setting. Psychological and behavioral variables—including mental fatigue, recovery, perceived ability, injury risk perception, and risk-taking behaviors —were assessed before each match, while perceived match load was recorded immediately after match completion. This protocol ensured accurate and unbiased baseline data for subsequent injury risk analyses. Follow-up survey Participants were recruited prior to the start of the 2023–2024 competitive season. 100-unit increase was associated with a 12% increase in injury risk (OR = 1.12, 95% CI: 0.98–1.29), which was not statistically significant (p = 0.06). Perceived risk level demonstrated a negligible difference (5.02%), and each unit increase in perceived risk was associated with a non-significant 7% increase in injury risk (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 0.83–1.38, p = 0.61), suggesting that abstract risk perception—unanchored by prior injury experience—failed to translate into protective behavioral regulation in this cohort. Conversely, risk-taking behaviors showed a significant difference, with a 15.02% increase, and a 54% increase in injury risk per unit increase (OR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.03–2.32), statistically significant (p < 0.05) (Table 2). Discussion This study aimed to investigate how training load, recovery quality, mental fatigue, perceived injury risk, risk-taking behaviors, and estimated athletic ability affect injury risk among adolescent soccer players. The main findings demonstrated that poorer recovery quality, greater engagement in risk-taking behaviors, and overestimation of athletic ability were each significantly associated with increased odds of sustaining a match- related injury in this cohort of adolescent soccer players. Among adolescent soccer players aged 14–17, 47.5% sustained new injuries, with an average of 0.65 injuries per player and an overall match injury incidence of 24.9 per 1,000 h of match exposure. This incidence is more than that reported in a systematic review by Robles-Palazón, et al.3, who found an average of 14.43 injuries per 1,000 match hours in male and female youth (≤ 19 years old) soccer players. In another review, Mandorino, et al40. also reported a wide range (2.84 to 47.7 per 1,000 h) in elite adolescent players, and Faude, et al 2. reported rates of 15–20 per 1,000 match hours in older adolescents. Such differences may reflect variation in competition level (elite vs. non-elite), age, and methodology. The lower injury incidence in our study may be due to the non- elite competition level, lower match intensity, and differences in exposure measurement methods. These factors should be considered when comparing injury rates across studies. Of the 26 injuries recorded, 61.5% were minimal (1–3 days of time loss), followed by mild (23.1%), moderate (11.5%), and severe (3.8%). These results align with Robles-Palazón, et al 3. and Faude, et al. 2, both of whom noted a predominance of minor injuries. Injury location data revealed that the most commonly affected sites were the thigh (30.77%), lower leg/Achilles tendon (19.23%), knee (15.38%), and ankle (15.38%), consistent with prior studies2,3,41. There was no significant difference in match load between injured and uninjured players, nor was there a clear association with injury risk. This contrasts with studies in adult populations 11,42,43, which found strong correlations between training loads and injury. The discrepancy may arise from age-related physiological differences, variations in measurement (e.g., subjective vs. objective load indicators), and our focus solely on match load rather than total load (training + matches) in our study than previous studies Gabbett and Domrow11and Anderson, et al. 42. These findings support the need for age-appropriate load management strategies that account for the developmental and contextual demands of adolescent athletes. Adolescent soccer players who remained injury-free reported significantly higher Total Quality Recovery (TQR) scores following both training sessions and games compared to those who sustained injuries. A one-point increase in the TQR score was associated with a 25% reduction in injury risk. These findings are consistent with Timoteo, et al 12. and Debien, et al. 44, which showed that lower recovery levels and declining TQR scores are Variable Non injured Injured t p-value Binary logistic regression generalized estimating equations B S. observation, reliance on coach-rated discrepancy calculations, and self-reported injury history (player and parent/guardian) rather than verified medical records, which may introduce recall bias—though dual reporting likely enhanced accuracy. Future studies should employ a priori power calculations, incorporate maturation metrics, expand surveillance to training contexts, and, where feasible, verify injury data through objective records. Conclusion This study found that overestimation of athletic ability, engagement in risk-taking behaviors, and poorer recovery quality were each significantly associated with increased odds of match-related injury in this cohort of adolescent soccer players. Unlike findings in adults, mental fatigue and perceived injury risk were not significant predictors in this young group, and match load alone did not predict match-related injury either. These results suggest the need for a comprehensive prevention approach that promotes realistic self-assessment, safe behaviors, and effective recovery strategies. Collaboration among coaches, trainers, and sports psychologists is essential to protect young athletes’ health and improve injury prevention. Future research should involve larger samples, longer follow-ups, and broader load monitoring to better understand match-related injury risk in youth soccer. Kelshaw, PhD, ATC 2,6 , Sanja Avramovic, PhD 2,7 , and Shane V. Caswell, PhD, ATC 2,4 Objective To investigate sex differences in sports-related concussion (SRC) rates among early adolescents participating in sex-comparable middle school (MS) sports. Study design This prospective epidemiological study was conducted as part of the Advancing Health Care Ini- tiatives for Underserved Students project in Virginia from 2015 to 2022. Athletic trainers collected injury and athlete exposure (AE) data from athletes MS athletes participating in sex-comparable sports, including baseball/softball, basketball, soccer, and track and field. Outcomes included SRC injury rates (IR)/1000 AE, IR ratios (IRRs) for overall sex and event-type differences (competition vs practice), and injury proportion ratios for injury mechanisms. Results A total of 11,213 athletes (girls, n = 5647; boys, n = 5566) contributed 329,269 AEs, during which 97 SRCs were diagnosed (0.29/1000 AE). Girls were more than twice as likely as boys to sustain an SRC overall (IRR, 2.26). In 3 of the 4 sex-comparable MS sports, girls had higher SRC rates in competition and practice than boys: softball/ baseball (competition/practice IRR, 4.19/2.35), basketball (3.77/2.74), and soccer (1.75/4.92). No sex differences were observed in track and field or in the proportional distribution of SRC mechanisms. Conclusions Among early adolescents participating in sex-comparable MS sports, girls were more than twice as likely as boys to sustain a SRC. The magnitude of the sex difference in SRC rates observed among MS athletes exceeded that previously reported in high school and collegiate populations. These findings demonstrate that sex-based differences in SRC risk are evident by early adolescence and highlight the need for developmentally appropriate, female-specific concussion prevention and clinical care strategies. N early 30 million school-age children participate in organized sports each year in the US. 1 Sports-related concussions (SRCs) are a prevalent injury, with estimates indicating that between 1.1 and 1.9 million US children suffer a sports- or recreation-related concussion annually. 2 Numerous studies have documented the incidence of SRCs among high school and collegiate athletes. Many report female athletes to have higher SRC rates than males in comparable sports at both high school and collegiate levels. 3–12 These sex differences in SRC rates have been attributed to variations in a range of factors, including biomechanical, hormonal, cognitive, psychological, and sociocultural influences. 4,13 Although substantial evidence exists regarding SRC in older adolescents and young adults, research on sex differences in SRC incidence among middle school (MS)-aged children (ages 10-13) remains limited, despite this age group representing the largest segment of organized sports participants in the US. 1 Presently, it remains uncertain whether the sex differences observed in older athletes apply to early adolescents. Closing this knowledge gap is critical, because the significant physical, cognitive, and psychosocial changes that occur alongside emerging sex differences during early adolescence may require tailored preventive strategies and care considerations. 14,15 Recognizing this gap, the Concussion in Sport Group, in its most recent consensus statement, called for greater representation of both younger and female athletes in SRC research. 16 Therefore, the purpose of this study was to investigate potential sex differences in SRC rates among early adolescent children participating in sex-comparable MS sports. Building on previous research, we hypothesized that MS girls would have significantly higher concussion rates than their male counterparts. From the 1

The primary physical event that caused the SRC, was classified as either direct contact with a ball, player, surface, field equipment, or nonspecific contact.
